recipe.history:
The bánh mì sandwich is a product of one of the most consequential colonial food encounters in culinary history. When France colonized Vietnam in the mid-nineteenth century, French bakers introduced the baguette — made from the wheat flour that the colonial administration imported, as Vietnamese cuisine had been built almost entirely on rice. Vietnamese bakers adapted the baguette recipe to their climate, substituting some wheat flour with rice flour, which created a lighter, thinner-crusted roll with an airier crumb — arguably more delicious than its French antecedent. Into this bread, Vietnamese cooks layered the flavors of their own culinary tradition: pickled daikon and carrot (đồ chua), fresh cucumber, cilantro, jalapeño, and rich spreads like pâté or liver mousse borrowed from French charcuterie, alongside pork preparations from Vietnamese tradition. The result was a sandwich that belonged entirely to neither cuisine but synthesized both into something new and astonishing.

Bánh mì arrived in the United States with Vietnamese refugees and immigrants after the fall of Saigon in 1975. Bakeries and sandwich shops opened in Vietnamese communities in cities like San Jose, Houston, and New Orleans, and the bánh mì became known to a wider American audience through the sheer force of its quality and its remarkable affordability. By the 2000s it was recognized by food media as one of the world's great sandwiches. The bánh mì burger fuses this tradition with American burger culture: a beef patty in place of the cold cuts, a baguette-style roll in place of the brioche, and the full complement of pickled vegetables, fresh herbs, sriracha mayo, and jalapeño that define the original. The result is bright, spicy, fatty, and acidic all at once.

I first ate a proper bánh mì at a tiny shop on the east side of a city I was visiting for work — the kind of place with a line out the door at 10am and a handwritten menu on the wall. I paid three dollars and stood on the sidewalk eating it in four minutes flat. The crunch of the pickled vegetables against the creamy spread and the heat of the jalapeño was something I had not encountered in a handheld form before. I started putting those pickles on burgers the following weekend, and adding sriracha mayo, and eventually building the whole structure around a baguette-style roll. Every time I make this burger I'm back on that sidewalk.

The bánh mì burger must be cooked to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit at the center — because the pickled vegetables and sriracha mayo are aggressive, acidic, and bright, and they need a rich, fatty, juicy counterweight. A well-done patty is dry and dense; the pickled daikon and carrot have nothing to work against and the whole sandwich becomes one-dimensional. A medium-rare patty is full of juice and fat, and when you bite through the crunch of the baguette roll and the vegetables and hit that pink, yielding interior, every element justifies itself. Medium rare is the architecture that holds this cross-cultural construction upright.
ingredients: 1 egg white + 1 tbsp water (wash for crust)
For the pickled daikon and carrot (đồ chua):
1 cup daikon radish, peeled and julienned
1/2 English cucumber, thinly sliced on the bias
2 jalapeños, thinly sliced into rounds (seeds in for heat, removed for less)
4 thin slices of liver pâté or omit if preferred
instructions: 1. Make the pickled daikon and carrot (start at least 1 hour ahead, or overnight for best flavor): Toss julienned daikon and carrot with 1 tsp salt; let sit 10 minutes. Rinse and squeeze out excess moisture. Combine rice wine vinegar, warm water, sugar, and remaining salt; stir until dissolved. Pack vegetables into a jar and pour brine over. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate. Ready in 1 hour, best after 4 hours.

2. Make the baguette-style rolls: Dissolve yeast and sugar in warm water; bloom 10 minutes. Combine bread flour, rice flour, and salt. Add yeast mixture and oil; mix with a dough hook on medium 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Dough should be slightly stiffer than brioche.

3. Cover and rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 4 equal pieces. Shape each into a 6-inch oval roll by flattening, folding the sides in, and rolling into a log with a taper at each end. Place seam-side down on a parchment-lined baking sheet; proof 45–60 minutes.

4. Preheat oven to 450°F (230°C) with a cast-iron pan on the bottom rack. Score the top of each roll with one long slash using a sharp knife or lame. Add 1 cup water to the bottom pan for steam; immediately slide rolls in. Bake 18–20 minutes until deeply golden with a crackly, thin crust. Cool on rack.
5. Make the sriracha mayo: Whisk together mayonnaise, sriracha, lime juice, fish sauce, and garlic powder. Adjust heat to preference. Refrigerate.

6. Season the patties: In a bowl, combine ground beef with garlic, fish sauce, soy sauce, sesame oil, black pepper, and salt. Mix gently with your hands until just combined — do not overwork. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into oval patties to match the shape of the rolls, about 3/4-inch thick. Press a center dimple.
7. Heat a cast-iron skillet or grill pan over high heat until smoking. Add neutral oil.
8. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes until deeply crusted and caramelized. Flip once. Cook 2–3 more minutes until center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C). Rest on a rack 3 minutes.
9. Slice baguette rolls lengthwise, not cutting all the way through. Open flat and press gently on the cut surface in the hot skillet for 60 seconds to toast lightly.
10. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of sriracha mayo on both cut surfaces of each roll. On the bottom, lay thin slices of pâté if using.
11. Place the rested patty on the roll. Drizzle with a few drops of Maggi seasoning sauce.
12. Layer cucumber slices, a generous pile of drained pickled daikon and carrot, jalapeño rounds, and a full sprig of fresh cilantro on top of the patty.
13. Fold the top of the roll over and press firmly to compress slightly — a true bánh mì-style sandwich holds its fillings by compression. Serve immediately while the crust is crackling.
